Pilot Summary: Weekly Planning Note for Support Handoffs

What we tested
The pilot tested whether a weekly planning note would help the four support teams coordinate handoffs.

Main feedback
In the end-of-pilot survey, most respondents said the note made ownership clearer. Several also said it duplicated information already in the ticket system.

Participation
- Each team tried the note for six weeks.
- Two teams skipped several weeks during a staffing shortage, so use was uneven.
- The survey went to all participating staff, and 19 of 31 people responded.

Limitation
We did not compare ticket resolution times before and after the pilot, so we cannot say whether the note made work faster.

Next decision
The operations group will decide whether to continue the pilot after reviewing feedback with team leads. No decision has been made yet.

Subject: A simple way to keep track of greenhouse watering

Hi everyone,

Watering in the greenhouse has become inconsistent, and I'd like to propose a light fix. I'm suggesting this as an idea, not as something we've already adopted.

What's not working now
- I first wrote notes on the whiteboard, but people erased them when they needed the board for other work.
- We now have a shared folder, but not everyone checks it before coming in.
- Several of you have offered to take turns, but nobody can see which days are covered. Sometimes two people water on the same day and then nobody comes the next day.

Why "water more often" isn't the answer
The plants haven't all been affected in the same way, so a general reminder hasn't helped.
- The east beds dry out faster than the others, especially after a sunny day. The seedlings there were wilting last week.
- The tomatoes near the south wall were already damp, so watering everything more often because of the east beds would be a mistake.

What I'm proposing
1. A simple shared schedule, kept in one predictable place, so anyone can see which days are already covered. That would help us avoid doubled-up days and gaps.
2. A short note for each bed, or for the beds that need attention, saying what it needs. For example, the east beds may need checking after sunny days, and the south-wall tomatoes may not need water if they're still damp.

I'd like to keep this light. It shouldn't become a complicated tracking system or a set of rules to follow exactly. The aim is to help whoever is there see what needs attention without adding another chore, and to leave room for them to use their own judgment.

If you have thoughts on where the schedule should live, or on what the bed notes should say, please let me know.

Thanks,
[Name]

Interim update: Coastal water sampling found elevated nitrate at three sites after heavy rain, but the source remains unknown.

Between June and August, the coastal survey team collected water samples at 12 sites. Sampling did not take place every week, as storms and unsafe boat conditions led to cancellations.

Lab analysis showed elevated nitrate at three sites following heavy rain. At two of those sites, readings returned closer to the earlier range by the next visit.

The samples were too limited to establish where the nitrate came from, so these results should not be read as identifying or resolving any pollution issue.

The team has not yet completed the autumn sampling round. These findings are being shared with watershed partners as an interim update and should not be treated as a full seasonal assessment.

Proposal: A four-week trial of a shared request list

The current problem
We keep losing track of requests that come in through the shared mailbox. People generally answer the customer, but the rest of the team cannot always tell whether anyone is working on a given request. On busy days, two people sometimes draft replies to the same message.

The proposal
I think we could try a simple shared list for four weeks. It would sit alongside the mailbox, not replace it. The aim of the trial is to find out whether the extra step is worthwhile.

How the list would work
- Whoever takes a request adds a line with the customer reference, a short description, their name, and the next action.
- The customer's full message would not go in the list.
- Anything waiting on a customer stays on the list with that status.
- We would also record when a reply has been sent, because a sent email does not necessarily mean the underlying request is finished.
- The morning shift reviews open items at the start of the day.
- We could use the existing team spreadsheet. I have not yet checked whether its current permissions are suitable, so that needs to be confirmed before we start. If they are not suitable, we would need another option.

How we would decide whether to keep it
At the end of the four weeks, we would compare duplicate replies and ask the team how much upkeep the list needed. If it creates more work than it saves, we could drop it.

Decision for you
I would like your view on whether we should run this trial, and, if so, whether the team spreadsheet is an acceptable home for the list once its permissions have been checked.

Proposal: Evening Opening of the Reading Room – Eight-Week Trial

Recommendation

I propose that the committee approve an eight-week trial in which the reading room stays open until eight on two evenings a week, Tuesday and Thursday. No start date should be announced until volunteer coverage, the cost estimate and insurance cover are settled (see "Before launch" below).

Why try it

Several people have asked for somewhere quiet to go after work, and our present closing time of five makes that difficult. The evidence of demand is modest. Seven residents supported the idea at the last open meeting, but that meeting was small, and we have no reliable count of how many people would actually attend. That uncertainty is the reason for proposing a limited trial rather than a permanent change.

Tuesday and Thursday seem the most workable evenings because the room has no regular bookings then. It seats eighteen people.

Practical requirements

- Volunteers: One volunteer would need to be present throughout each evening, with a second available as backup. Three people have said they are interested in helping, but none has committed to a rota.
- Costs: There would be some extra heating and lighting costs. The facilities team thinks they may be modest in spring, but it has not given an estimate.
- Insurance: We need to confirm that the building's insurance covers the proposed hours.

Before launch

Volunteer coverage, the cost estimate and insurance confirmation should all be settled before we announce a start date.

Assessing the trial

I suggest we record attendance at every session and ask users whether the hours were useful. At the end of the eight weeks, we can compare attendance with the extra cost. A busy first night would be encouraging, but it would not show whether demand lasts, so the full run of figures matters more. The committee can then discuss the results before deciding on any longer arrangement.

Fallback

If coverage cannot be found for both nights, we could consider opening on one evening instead. That is not part of this proposal and would need a separate decision.

I used to think repairing old radios was mostly about patience and a steady hand. It is, a little. But what keeps me coming back is the moment a station slips through the static, especially when I have no idea what language I'm hearing.

I'm not an expert, and I still make mistakes I can hear the second I put the case back together. Last winter I spent three evenings chasing a loose connection that turned out to be a tired switch.

The radio works now. I keep the switch in a jar on my desk, mostly as a reminder not to get too pleased with myself.

I planted the peas early because the forecast looked kind, and the forecast, for once, kept its promise. The first shoots appeared along the back fence a few days later, thin as green thread. I put in the strings on Saturday, though one leans enough that I may have to call it a design choice.

The tomatoes are still sulking in their pots, which may be my fault; I moved them outside before the nights warmed up. They have not given up, exactly, but they have made their opinion clear. I brought them back under the porch when the temperature dipped.

A neighbor told me the basil would be less dramatic. So far it is simply sitting there, which I suppose counts as a point in its favor. The pot is still by the kitchen door, where I can remember to bring it in.

Next weekend I will try again, with less confidence and more fleece. If the tomatoes recover, I will claim I planned the whole experiment.

I finally got round to fixing the little bench by the back door. It had been wobbling for months, and every time I sat down to take my boots off I thought, yes, I really should do something about that. On Sunday I did. One new screw, a bit of glue, and a surprisingly long search for the clamp I was certain I owned.

It still looks like a bench that has spent twelve years outside, which is fine by me. I gave it a quick sand where the wood was catching on sleeves, but I left the old paint alone. The cat has already claimed it again, so I reckon the repair has passed its most demanding inspection.

Visitors need to reserve a seat at least one business day ahead. A reservation helps the archive prepare the reading room, but it does not request or hold specific collection items. Researchers looking for fragile or oversized materials should contact staff in advance.

Walk-ins may be admitted if space allows, but staff cannot promise access to a particular collection without advance notice. Some materials are stored off site and may need additional time to retrieve.

The room is closed on public holidays. The archive website lists closure dates and the reservation form; visitors who need to change a booking can contact the reading room directly.

I bought a secondhand sewing machine because I wanted to mend my own clothes. A sensible ambition. Then I spent an entire Sunday making one trouser leg shorter than the other. The machine behaved perfectly; I would like to make that clear before anyone blames the machine.

By the next weekend I had learned to mark the hem before cutting, and to try the trousers on with both shoes. Small discoveries, apparently available to everyone except me. I still take difficult repairs to the tailor, but I can now fix a loose seam without turning it into a larger emergency. That feels like progress, even if my first attempt is living at the back of the wardrobe.

Subject: Bicycle storage proposal – where things stand after Tuesday's meeting

Dear residents,

At Tuesday's residents meeting, we discussed moving bicycle storage from the entrance hall to the unused laundry room. I'm writing to summarise where things stand, especially for those who couldn't attend, and to suggest how we move forward.

**The proposal**
Move bicycle storage from the entrance hall to the unused laundry room.

**What was discussed**
- Several people supported the idea because bikes in the entrance hall currently make it difficult to reach the noticeboard.
- Others were concerned about carrying bikes down the short flight of steps to the laundry room.

**What is unclear**
Near the end of the discussion, the chair said we should try the laundry room once the old cabinets were removed. I understood this as agreement to go ahead with a trial, but two residents came away thinking we had agreed only to look into the option. The notes taken during the meeting say, "Laundry room option to be explored." Since people understood the outcome differently, we should treat the proposal as not yet settled.

**Current status**
- The current entrance-hall storage remains in use.
- Please don't move any bikes or furniture yet.
- The building caretaker can check whether the old cabinets are still needed, but no one has been assigned to arrange their removal.
- We have not yet discussed access for residents who cannot manage the steps.

**Next steps**
1. Confirm what was decided: a trial, or further exploration only.
2. Decide who will arrange removal of the cabinets, if they are not needed.
3. Discuss access for residents who cannot manage the steps.

**Your input**
If you missed the meeting, I hope this gives you a clear picture of the proposal. Please reply with any practical concerns or suggestions, particularly about the steps or access, so we can consider them before anything changes.

Thank you,
[Name]

Summary: The planning group discussed a revised chart on Monday, but the record does not confirm whether it was the version with projected costs or the version without them.

Sequence of events
1. After the first review, Mira sent the revised chart to Leon. Leon had asked for a version without the projected costs. Her message said the labels had been updated. It did not name the file version or say whether projections were included.
2. Leon forwarded the chart to the planning group. His note said the numbers were still provisional. The email thread included a link to the chart. The group had also received an earlier chart that included projected costs, attached to a previous message.
3. On Monday, the group used the chart in its discussion. The notes mention the revised labels and the provisional figures. They do not give a filename or say which copy was shown on screen.

What is established
- Mira sent the revised chart to Leon.
- Leon forwarded it to the planning group.
- The group was told the numbers were provisional and that the labels had been updated.

What is not confirmed
- Which version the group looked at on Monday: the revised chart, which Leon requested without projections, or the earlier chart with projected costs.
- Whether the revised chart actually excluded projections. Mira's message did not say.

Suggested follow-up: Ask Mira to confirm the filename and whether the revised chart includes projections. Ask whoever presented on Monday which copy was on screen.

The community kitchen is available for private bookings on Saturdays from 10 a.m. to 4 p.m. The hire fee is $110 for that six-hour period. A refundable cleaning deposit of $60 is collected separately and returned after the caretaker checks the room. The booking is not confirmed until both payments have been received.

Bookings include use of the oven, refrigerator, worktables, and twelve dining chairs. The pantry cupboard is reserved for the weekly meal program and must remain closed. Guests must bring their own ingredients, serving dishes, and dish towels. The dishwasher can be used, but its final cycle must finish before departure.

Groups may have up to sixteen people in the kitchen at one time, including children and organizers. This limit comes from the room's approved layout and is different from the number of dining chairs. Events involving food sales require the organizer to contact the local licensing office; kitchen hire does not itself grant permission to sell food.

Cancel at least seven days before the booking to receive a refund of the hire fee. Later cancellations forfeit the hire fee, but the cleaning deposit is returned if the room has not been used. The caretaker can answer equipment questions by email and normally replies within two working days. We cannot promise a same-day response.
